extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century reading public; clergy/sermon-writers and polite society
extracted.subtask_description: Short prescriptive guidance drawn from Spectator essays on three related domains: religious/musical worship and sermon-writing (eloquence), public decorum (behaviour in church, responding to solicitations), and personal politeness (cleanliness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to solicitations for public office
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to the People who want a Place, there are none to be pitied more than those who are solicited for one. A plain Answer, with a Denial in it, is looked upon as Pride, and a civil Answer as a Promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that requests for preferment create awkward expectations: a curt refusal will be judged proud, a civil reply taken as a promise. The essay illustrates the absurdity of claims for reward by publishing many petitions (e.g., men asking for honours for trivial or scandalous 'merits'), implying one should avoid encouraging baseless claims and be cautious about how replies will be read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate church music (Musical Sacrifice and Adoration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical Sacrifice and Adoration has claimed a Place in the Laws and Customs of the most different Nations...no one can have the least Reason for Disaffection to that solemn kind of Melody which consists of the Praises of our Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer modest, devotional music in public worship: a 'Voluntary before the first Lesson' prepares the congregation and calms tumults, and an Anthem can relieve languishing spirits and deepen devotion. While pompous foreign music may affect the senses, modest English practice (softening sublime poetry in moving strains) is laudable because it humbles or exalts the soul appropriately and leads worshippers into piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful behaviour in church / opposition to 'Rattling Clubs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Vociferous 'Rattling Clubs' invading the Church, making loud signals, conferring together during sermons, and propagating noise through the pews are rude and destructive of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict composure and steadiness of thought in sacred services. Laughter in sacred transactions is 'far less pardonable' than mere whining at a conventicle; noisy, organised mockery during sermons destroys comprehension for all and offends decency. Ministers and congregations should resist and not encourage such turbulent behaviour; those who interrupt or mimic the pulpit display folly and contempt of heaven and earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness as a mark of politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanliness is a Mark of Politeness: no one, unadorn'd with this Virtue, can go into Company without giving a manifest Offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal neatness and cleanliness are expected social signals of civility; the more elevated one's social position, the more this duty arises. Different nations are distinguished by cleanliness as much as by arts and sciences. Practically: attend to dress, linen, and general outward neatness to avoid offence in company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness as a foster-mother of love
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanliness may be said to be the Foster-Mother of Love. Beauty produces passion, but Cleanliness preserves it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular neatness and care of person maintain attractiveness and attachment: an indifferent person kept perpetually neat can win hearts from a pretty slattern. Age preserved in cleanliness remains amiable. Thus personal cleanliness has direct social and romantic utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness as analogy to purity of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanliness bears Analogy to Purity of Mind and naturally inspires refined Sentiments and Passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surroundings and outward habits shape inner thought: familiar exposure to pure and unsullied objects suggests pure thoughts, whereas vice loses horror by familiarity. Observances of washing and purification (as in Jewish and Mahometan rites) typify inward purity. Anecdotal anti-example: neglecting simple washings led to progressive misfortunes in a dervise story, underscoring the moral and practical importance of outward cleanliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid whimsical adherence to numerical symmetry in literary form
rubrics_metrics.description: The Love of Symmetry and Order betrays him sometimes into very whimsical Fancies...it was perhaps a Thought of the like Nature which determined Homer himself to divide each of his Poems into as many Books, as there are Letters in the Greek Alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let arbitrary numerical symmetry (e.g., number of books or sections) drive literary structure. Choosing a form solely because it is 'odd' or corresponds to a reputedly fortunate number (e.g., seven) is whimsy, not reasoned literary design. Structure should be driven by substantive considerations, not numerological prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence must move the affections and achieve the sublime ('Marvellous or Sublime')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another Part of Eloquence...I mean the Marvellous or Sublime. In this the Christian Orator has the Advantage beyond Contradiction...The Contemplation of such Objects will give our Discourse a noble Vigour, an invincible Force, beyond the Power of any human Consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A truly excellent orator aims first to move the affections; the sublime (marvellous) elevates imagination and feeling. To achieve it, treat great and glorious mysteries (resurrection, judgment, incarnation) which enlarge the mind and furnish material for powerful, exalted speech. Cultivate lofty conceptions to give discourse 'noble vigour' and to rouse hearers beyond mere moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Christian doctrines as superior material for persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity...as it brings the Consideration of another Life into the Question...is more adapted to affect the Minds of the Audience...the Motives to Persuasion under Christianity [are] greater than those which meer moral Considerations could supply us with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preaching, employ theological themes that present higher and longer-continued rewards and punishments: such stakes strengthen persuasive force. Moral commonplaces (profit/honesty) are useful but inferior; supernatural doctrine supplies weightier motives and broader imaginative scope for amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate St. Paul as a model of eloquence, but adapt to context
rubrics_metrics.description: That when he, under the Want of several Advantages of Nature...was heard, admired, and made a Standard to succeeding Ages by the best Judge...our Clergy may learn, That...St. Paul's Harangues...have given them a noble Example of, and the Christian Religion has furnished them with certain Means of attaining to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study St. Paul's discourses (e.g., Corinthians, his speech before Agrippa, his treatment of resurrection) as exemplars of powerful Christian oratory. Note, however, Paul sometimes confines himself in certain settings (Athens) to strict argument because of local laws and customs—so adapt rhetorical method to audience and legal/contextual limits while seeking Paul's fervour and use of grand themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt rhetoric to audience and institutional/legal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: In his Reasonings upon Idolatry at Athens...he confines himself to strict Argument only; but...all Attempts upon the Affections and Strokes of Oratory were expressly forbidden, by the Laws of that Country, in Courts of Judicature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective speakers must recognise and conform to local norms and legal limits: certain forums ban appeals to the passions or particular rhetorical devices. Choose style and methods appropriate to the setting; where laws limit emotional appeals, rely on rigorous argumentation instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical doctrines should refine and exalt human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the common Boast of the Heathen Philosophers, that by the Efficacy of their several Doctrines, they made Humane Nature resemble the Divine...the Design was great and glorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophies and moral systems by whether they refine, exalt, and improve rational character toward a divine standard. The highest value of invention and imagination lies in works that refine and exalt the rational mind rather than mere novelty or entertainment.
